source.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets
source.authors: Alethea Power; Yuri Burda; Harrison Edwards; Igor Babuschkin; Vedant Misra

record.tranche_reason: Tests generalization dynamics and interventions on small algorithmic datasets, a new setting relative to the natural-data claim.
record.gate_note: The study uses abstract-symbol binary operations rather than natural data. It does not test any version as specified; cited results from other work are not extracted as rows. Figure-only comparisons are recorded only where the text states their outcome.
record.test_reason: The study reports related generalization phenomena on algorithmic tasks, but none measures a claim version as specified. Late generalization is not a width sweep; random-label outliers are not a fully random-label control; the intervention experiments lack the required optimizer, classifier, or fixed-epoch comparisons; and the sharpness experiment does not measure gap rankings within a convolutional family.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: small algorithmic tasks can exhibit generalization long after memorization; smaller datasets require substantially longer optimization; weight decay improves data efficiency; and a preliminary sharpness experiment suggests an association with generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Small transformer on abstract-symbol algorithmic datasets; experiments include Adam without weight decay and AdamW/regularization variants. The study explicitly says its effects are more pronounced than on natural data.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization depends on dataset size, operation symmetry/complexity, learning-rate choice, weight decay and optimization noise; larger training sets make train and validation curves track more closely.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation accuracy can rise from chance to nearly perfect long after training accuracy becomes nearly perfect; success varies across operations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small transformers can exhibit delayed generalization on some algorithmic binary-operation tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Near 25–30% training data, a one-percentage-point reduction increases median time to generalization by 40–50%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing algorithmic training data can sharply increase the optimization needed for generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay more than halves the samples needed relative to most tested interventions; some optimization noise helps and learning rate requires narrow tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization and data efficiency on the S5 task depend strongly on optimization and regularization choices.

fits_no_version.finding: All outlier experiments eventually attain 100% training accuracy; up to 1000 outliers have little effect, while larger corruption narrows the training-data fractions permitting generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Algorithmic generalization can coexist with memorized label exceptions, but becomes harder as exceptions increase.

fits_no_version.finding: Keskar sharpness and validation accuracy have Spearman correlation −0.79548, with p < 0.000014, across initialization seeds on S5 composition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower sharpness correlates with higher validation accuracy in a preliminary algorithmic-transformer experiment.

record.problems: The main experiments use small algorithmic datasets and one small transformer architecture, limiting direct relevance to natural-data claims. Some comparisons are presented only in figures, and the sharpness investigation is described as preliminary.
record.rows_left_out: The text reports additional operation-specific curves and optimizer variants in Figures 2 and 6, but does not provide recoverable per-condition numeric values or separate prose outcomes for each; these are not reconstructed as individual result rows.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fully randomized-label training, including held-out chance performance for random labels.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning on image or language benchmarks.
Batch-size comparisons under equal epoch budgets and recipe adaptations on image classifiers or language models.
Dropout effects in fully connected or convolutional classifiers, including training-set size, excessive dropout, and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness ranking training–test gaps among convolutional networks with similarly low training loss, and comparison against norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and measuring retrained test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T3 classification conflicts with its correctly unlinked rows. All row states here are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; this does not dispute the reported algorithmic-task findings.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test memorization of arbitrary labels alongside generalization on natural labels.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison.
Optimizer comparisons use small algorithmic datasets, not image-classification or language benchmarks as specified.
No large-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets on image classifiers or language models.
Dropout is tried on an algorithmic task, not the specified classifier regimes or training-set conditions.
Measures sharpness on an algorithmic task; does not test magnitude-aware perturbations or compare gap rankings among convolutional networks.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain image classifiers.

rows.subject: small transformer
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads, about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Adam without weight decay on modular division; training and validation accuracy measured through optimization
rows.measure: Training and validation accuracy over optimization steps
rows.value: Training accuracy becomes close to perfect at < 103 optimization steps; validation accuracy takes close to 106 steps to reach that level, with very little evidence of generalization until 105 steps
rows.note: Algorithmically generated equations with abstract-symbol operands, not natural data.
rows.check: The reported late generalization is supported, but does not test natural versus fully randomized labels or widening beyond interpolation. Render optimization steps as powers: <10^3, approximately 10^6, and approximately 10^5.

rows.subject: small transformer
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads, about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Trained on binary-operation datasets at varying training-data fractions; validation accuracy measured

conditions.value: variety of binary operations in Appendix A.1.1

rows.value: Figure 2 (right); text says some operations did not generalize within the allowed budget at any percentage of data up to 95%
rows.note: Exact plotted values are figure-only. The text names x3 + xy2 + y (mod 97) as an operation that did not generalize within the budget.
rows.check: Operation-dependent generalization does not measure any version. This aggregates successful and unsuccessful operations, so a single partial state is also misleading. The budget is 10^5 updates.

rows.subject: small transformer
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads, about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared full-batch Adam, Adam variants, AdamW weight decay, residual dropout, and Gaussian noise variants on the S5 product task

conditions.value: different optimization algorithms and regularization variants

rows.value: Weight decay improves generalization the most; adding weight decay has a very large effect on data efficiency, more than halving the samples needed compared to most other interventions
rows.note: The text gives the comparative conclusion, but values for individual plotted variants are not recoverable from the supplied text.
rows.check: The weight-decay benefit is supported, but does not establish Adam versus SGD performance or dropout benefits in fully connected or convolutional classifiers. The listed optimizers are Adam/AdamW variants; full-batch Adam is not ordinary gradient descent. The budget is 10^5 updates.

rows.subject: small transformer
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads, about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Added optimization noise using minibatches or Gaussian noise to weights or updates

conditions.value: minibatch gradient noise or Gaussian noise applied to weights or updates

rows.value: Adding some noise to the optimization process is beneficial for generalization
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative outcome, without separate values for each noise variant.
rows.check: Qualitative benefits from optimization noise do not establish a large-batch penalty under equal epoch budgets. This is not evidence for a partial version-level effect.

rows.subject: small transformer
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads, about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Varied learning rate in Adam variants
rows.value: Learning rate had to be tuned in a relatively narrow window for generalization to happen (within 1 order of magnitude)
rows.note: Suboptimal hyperparameter choice severely limits generalization, as also stated in the Figure 2 caption.
rows.check: Learning-rate sensitivity within Adam variants does not compare adaptive methods against SGD. The stated narrow tuning window is supported.

rows.subject: small transformer
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads, about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-data fraction and measured optimization steps until validation accuracy first exceeded 99% on S5 product
rows.measure: Median optimization steps to validation accuracy > 99%
rows.value: In the vicinity of 25-30% of data, a decrease of 1% of training data leads to an increase of 40-50% in median time to generalization
rows.note: The optimization budget was increased to 5 · 105 steps for these experiments.
rows.check: The data-size versus learning-time result is supported, but no version concerns this relationship. The increased budget is 5 × 10^5 updates.

rows.subject: small transformer
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, width 128, 4 attention heads, about 4 · 10^5 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Introduced randomly relabeled outliers into the training set and measured generalization
rows.measure: Generalization performance / range of training-data percentages where models generalize
rows.value: The effect of introducing a small number of outliers (up to 1000) is not very pronounced
rows.note: The text states that all experiments reached 100% training accuracy; increasing outlier count decreases the range of training-data percentages for which models generalize.
rows.check: Fitting randomly relabeled outliers while generalizing on clean algorithmic validation data does not supply V1's natural-label and fully randomized-label comparison. It also does not remove influential memorized examples as V8 requires.

rows.subject: small transformer
rows.operation_detail: Introduced randomly relabeled outliers into the training set and measured generalization

conditions.value: large number, exact threshold not stated

rows.measure: Range of training-data percentages where models generalize
rows.value: Increasing k decreases the range of training data percentages for which the optimization procedure converges to models that generalize; a large number hinders generalization significantly
rows.note: The figure lists k ∈ [0, 10, 100, 1000, 2000, 3000], but the prose does not identify the exact onset of the larger effect.
rows.check: Increasing label corruption is neither V1's fully randomized-label control nor V8's removal-and-retraining intervention. The qualitative deterioration is supported, but no exact onset is stated.

rows.subject: networks trained on the S5 composition objective
rows.operation_detail: Measured Keskar et al. sharpness approximation φ and validation accuracy across trained networks

conditions.value: fixed number of steps; approximately half achieved high validation accuracy

rows.measure: Spearman correlation between validation accuracy and φ score
rows.note: Authors call this suggestive; they describe a preliminary investigation. This is a correlation with validation accuracy, not a direct comparison of training–test gaps or magnitude-aware sharpness.
rows.check: The reported correlation is correct, but validation accuracy versus Keskar sharpness across transformers does not measure V7's generalization-gap ranking within a convolutional family or its comparison with norm and margin measures. The supplied text does not establish whether the implemented perturbations were magnitude-aware; remove the record's categorical assertion that they were not.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
